title: Difference Amps, Integrators & Differentiators
description: Amplify the difference of two signals, and integrate or differentiate a signal with an op amp and a capacitor.

study.title: Difference amplifier
study.body: $v_2$ drives the − input through $R_1$ (feedback $R_2$); $v_1$ drives the + input through the divider $R_3$, $R_4$. If the ratios match, $R_4/R_3 = R_2/R_1$, the output depends only on the difference $v_1 - v_2$, and the common-mode signal is rejected. The input resistance seen by $v_1$ is $R_3 + R_4$.

study.title: Difference amplifier: general case
study.body: Use superposition. With $v_2 = 0$: $v_+ = v_1\frac{R_4}{R_3+R_4}$, amplified by the noninverting gain $1 + R_2/R_1$. With $v_1 = 0$: an inverting amplifier, $-(R_2/R_1)v_2$. Mismatched ratios leave a common-mode gain, so precision resistors (or an instrumentation amplifier) are used when the common-mode voltage is large.

study.title: Integrator
study.body: Replace $R_2$ of the inverting amplifier by a capacitor. The − input is a virtual ground, so $i = v_{in}/R$ flows into $C$ and $v_o = -v_C$. Integrating the capacitor current gives a running integral of the input. A reset switch across $C$ sets $v_o(0) = 0$.

study.title: Integrator responses
study.body: A constant input $V$ gives a ramp with slope $-V/RC$: $v_o(t) = -Vt/RC$, until the output saturates. A symmetric square wave of ±$V$ gives a triangle wave; each half-period $T/2$ changes the output by $VT/(2RC)$. Example: $V$ = 1 V, $R$ = 10 kΩ, $C$ = 0.1 µF ($RC$ = 1 ms): the output falls by 1 V every millisecond.

study.title: Differentiator
study.body: Swap the parts: $C$ at the input, $R$ in the feedback. The capacitor current $C\,dv_{in}/dt$ flows through $R$, so the output is proportional to the slope of the input. A ramp $v_{in} = St$ gives a constant $v_o = -RCS$; a sine of frequency $\omega$ is multiplied by $\omega RC$.

study.title: Pitfalls
study.body:
- Both circuits invert: watch the minus sign.
- An integrator keeps integrating any small dc offset or bias current until it saturates, so it needs a reset (or a large resistor across $C$).
- A differentiator's gain $\omega RC$ grows with frequency, so it amplifies high-frequency noise.
- Units: $RC$ is in seconds; 10 kΩ × 0.1 µF = 1 ms.

steps.title: Amplifying a difference
steps.body:
Feed $v_2$ to the − input through $R_1$ (feedback $R_2$) and $v_1$ to the + input through the divider $R_3$, $R_4$.
When $R_4/R_3 = R_2/R_1$ the output is proportional to $v_1 - v_2$ only. Anything common to both inputs is ignored.

steps.prompt: Difference amplifier with an ideal op amp. Tap every resistor that carries the **same current** as $R_1$.
steps.explanation: No current flows into the op-amp inputs. At the − input that leaves only one path for the current of $R_1$: it continues through the feedback resistor $R_2$. On the other side, $R_3$ and $R_4$ share a current with each other (they form a divider that sets $v_+$), but that current has nothing to do with $R_1$.

steps.prompt: A difference amplifier has $R_1 = R_3$ = {{R1|Ω}} and $R_2 = R_4$ = {{R2|Ω}}. With $v_1$ = {{v1|V}} and $v_2$ = {{v1-d|V}}, find $v_o$.
A matched difference amplifier ($R_2/R_1 = R_4/R_3$ = {{k}}) has both inputs at the same voltage, $v_1 = v_2$ = {{Vcm|V}}. What is $v_o$?
steps.explanation: $v_o = \frac{R_2}{R_1}(v_1 - v_2)$ = {{k}} × 0 = 0 V. A voltage common to both inputs (common-mode signal) is rejected; only the difference is amplified.

steps.title: The general case by superposition
steps.body:
- $v_1$ alone ($v_2$ = 0): the divider gives $v_+ = v_1\frac{R_4}{R_3+R_4}$, and the circuit is a noninverting amplifier with gain $1 + R_2/R_1$.
- $v_2$ alone ($v_1$ = 0): $v_+$ = 0, so it is an inverting amplifier with gain $-R_2/R_1$.
Add the two contributions.

steps.prompt: The resistors are **not** matched: $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}}, $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}}, $R_3$ = {{R3|Ω}}, $R_4$ = {{R4|Ω}}. With $v_1$ = {{v1|V}} and $v_2$ = {{v2|V}}, find $v_o$.
In a difference amplifier with $R_3$ = {{R3|Ω}} and $R_4$ = {{R4|Ω}}, what input resistance does source $v_1$ see?
steps.explanation: $v_1$ drives $R_3$ and $R_4$ in series to ground; the + input draws no current. So $R_{in,1} = R_3 + R_4$ = {{R3+R4|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: For the output of the difference amplifier to depend only on $v_1 - v_2$, the resistors must satisfy $R_4/R_3 = R_2/R_1$.
steps.explanation: True. Then $\frac{R_4}{R_3+R_4}\left(1+\frac{R_2}{R_1}\right) = \frac{R_2}{R_1}$, so both inputs get the same weight with opposite signs and a common-mode input cancels exactly.

steps.prompt: Why is a difference amplifier useful for a sensor connected through long wires?
options: Interference picked up equally on both wires is common-mode and gets rejected
It has infinite input resistance at both inputs
It has a larger gain than an inverting amplifier
It removes the need for negative feedback
steps.explanation: Hum or noise induced on a pair of wires is (nearly) the same on both, so it is a common-mode signal; the difference amplifier amplifies only the wanted difference. Its input resistances are finite ($R_3 + R_4$ for $v_1$), which is why instrumentation amplifiers add buffers in front.

steps.title: The integrator
steps.body:
Put a capacitor in the feedback path. The − input is a virtual ground, so $i = v_{in}/R$, and all of it charges $C$.
Since the left plate is at 0 V, $v_o = -v_C$, and the capacitor voltage is the integral of its current.

steps.prompt: In the integrator, why is $v_o = -v_C$ (with $v_C$ measured from the left plate to the right plate)?
options: The left plate is at virtual ground (0 V)
The output resistance of the op amp is zero
The input voltage appears across the capacitor
steps.explanation: KVL from the output through $C$ to the − input: the left plate sits at $v_-$ = 0 V, so $v_C = 0 - v_o$, i.e. $v_o = -v_C$.

steps.prompt: The integrator has $R$ = {{R|Ω}} and $C$ = {{C|F}}. The reset switch opens at $t = 0$ ($v_o(0) = 0$) and a constant $v_{in}$ = {{V|V}} is applied. Find $v_o$ at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
steps.explanation:
For a constant input the integral is just $Vt$: $v_o(t) = -\frac{V t}{RC}$.
$RC$ = {{R|Ω}} × {{C|F}} = {{R*C|s}}, so $v_o$ = −{{V}} × {{t|s}}/{{R*C|s}} = {{-V*t/(R*C)|V}}. The output ramps **down** for a positive input.

steps.title: The differentiator
steps.body:
Swap $R$ and $C$. The capacitor current is $C\,dv_{in}/dt$ (its right plate is at virtual ground), and it flows through $R$ to the output:
$v_o = 0 - R\cdot C\frac{dv_{in}}{dt}$

steps.prompt: A differentiator has $C$ = {{C|F}} and $R$ = {{R|Ω}}. The input is a ramp $v_{in}(t) = {{S}}\,t$ V ($t$ in seconds). Find $v_o$.
steps.explanation: $\frac{dv_{in}}{dt}$ = {{S}} V/s, so $v_o = -RC\frac{dv_{in}}{dt}$ = −{{R*C|s}} × {{S}} V/s = {{-R*C*S|V}}, a constant.

steps.prompt: Match each input to the output it produces
steps.explanation: Integrating a constant gives a ramp; integrating alternating constants (square wave) gives alternating ramps (triangle). Differentiation undoes this: the slope of a ramp is constant, and a triangle wave has alternating slopes, giving a square wave. All outputs are also inverted.

steps.prompt: A differentiator ($R$ = {{R|Ω}}, $C$ = {{C|F}}) has input $v_{in} = {{Vm}}\sin(2\pi f t)$ V with $f$ = {{f|Hz}}. What is the amplitude of $v_o$?
steps.explanation:
$\frac{d}{dt}V_m\sin\omega t = \omega V_m\cos\omega t$, so $v_o = -\omega RC V_m\cos\omega t$.
Amplitude: $\omega RCV_m$ = 2π × {{f|Hz}} × {{R*C|s}} × {{Vm|V}} = {{2*pi*f*R*C*Vm|V}}. It grows in proportion to frequency.

steps.prompt: A differentiator amplifies high-frequency noise much more than a low-frequency signal of the same amplitude.
steps.explanation: True. For a sine, the output amplitude is $\omega RC V_m$, proportional to frequency. Fast noise therefore dominates, which is why practical differentiators limit the high-frequency gain (e.g. with a small resistor in series with $C$).

steps.prompt: An integrator ($R$ = {{R|Ω}}, $C$ = {{C|F}}, $v_o(0)$ = 0) gets a constant input of {{V|V}}. The output saturates at −{{Vs|V}}. After how long does it saturate?
steps.explanation:
$|v_o(t)| = Vt/RC$ reaches $V_{sat}$ at $t = V_{sat}RC/V$.
$RC$ = {{R*C|s}}, so $t$ = {{Vs}} × {{R*C|s}}/{{V}} = {{Vs*R*C/V|s}}.

steps.prompt: Design an integrator with $R$ = {{R|Ω}} so that a constant input of {{V|V}} makes the output ramp down at {{S/1000}} V/ms. What capacitance is needed?
steps.explanation:
Slope magnitude: $\frac{V}{RC} = S$ → $C = \frac{V}{RS}$.
$S$ = {{S/1000}} V/ms = {{S}} V/s, so $C$ = {{V}}/({{R|Ω}} × {{S}} V/s) = {{V/(R*S)|F}}.

steps.prompt: A symmetric ±{{V|V}} square wave of frequency {{f|Hz}} drives an integrator with $R$ = {{R|Ω}} and $C$ = {{C|F}}. Find the peak-to-peak amplitude of the triangle wave at the output.
steps.explanation:
During each half-period $T/2 = 1/(2f)$ = {{1/(2*f)|s}} the input is constant, so the output ramps by $\frac{V}{RC}\cdot\frac{T}{2}$.
$V_{pp} = \frac{V}{2fRC}$ = {{V}}/(2 × {{f}} × {{R*C|s}}) = {{V/(2*f*R*C)|V}}.

steps.prompt: A differentiator ($R$ = {{R|Ω}}, $C$ = {{C|F}}) receives an input that rises linearly from 0 to {{Vp|V}} in {{T|s}}. What is $v_o$ during the rise?
steps.explanation:
Slope of the input: {{Vp|V}}/{{T|s}} = {{Vp/T}} V/s.
$v_o = -RC\frac{dv_{in}}{dt}$ = −{{R*C|s}} × {{Vp/T}} V/s = {{-R*C*Vp/T|V}}.

steps.prompt: An integrator ($R$ = {{R|Ω}}, $C$ = {{C|F}}) starts with $v_o(0)$ = {{V0|V}} (the capacitor is precharged). A constant input of {{V|V}} is applied at $t = 0$. Find $v_o$ at $t$ = {{t|s}}.
A constant positive voltage is applied to an ideal integrator (reset just released). How does the output behave?
options: It ramps down linearly until it saturates at the negative limit
It ramps up linearly until it saturates at the positive limit
It jumps to a constant negative value and stays there
It decays exponentially back to zero
steps.explanation: $v_o = -\frac{V}{RC}t$: a straight line with negative slope. The ideal circuit never settles; a real one stops when the op amp saturates near the negative supply.

steps.prompt: A bridge sensor gives $v_1$ = {{2.5+d|V|4}} and $v_2$ = 2.5 V. A matched difference amplifier with $R_2/R_1$ = {{k}} amplifies it. Find $v_o$.
steps.explanation:
$v_1 - v_2$ = {{d|V}}, the 2.5 V common-mode level is rejected.
$v_o = \frac{R_2}{R_1}(v_1 - v_2)$ = {{k}} × {{d|V}} = {{k*d|V}}.

steps.prompt: An integrator ($R$ = {{R|Ω}}, $C$ = {{C|F}}, $v_o(0) = 0$) receives a {{V|V}} pulse lasting {{t1|s}}, after which the input returns to 0 V. Find $v_o$ at $t$ = {{t1+0.003|s}}.
steps.explanation:
During the pulse the output ramps to $-\frac{V t_1}{RC}$ = −{{V}} × {{t1|s}}/{{R*C|s}} = {{-V*t1/(R*C)|V}}.
After the pulse $v_{in} = 0$, so no current flows into $C$ and the output **holds** that value: $v_o$ = {{-V*t1/(R*C)|V}}.

steps.prompt: A symmetric square wave (dashed) drives an ideal op-amp **integrator**, with $v_o$ = 0 at $t$ = 0. Which graph shows the output (solid)?
steps.explanation: The integrator output changes at the rate $dv_o/dt = -v_{in}/RC$. A constant positive input gives a straight line going **down**, a constant negative input a line going up, so the square wave becomes a triangle wave, starting downwards from 0. A triangle going up forgets the minus sign, an inverted square wave is a plain inverting amplifier, and the spikes at the edges are the response of a differentiator.

steps.prompt: An integrator with $R$ = {{R|Ω}} is driven by the square wave (dashed); the solid curve is its output. Find $C$.
steps.explanation: While the input is +{{V|V}}, the output falls along a straight line with slope $-V/RC$. Read that slope: in half a period, {{T/2|s}}, the output falls by {{sw|V}}. So $RC$ = {{V|V}} × {{T/2|s}} / {{sw|V}} = {{RC|s}}, and $C$ = {{RC|s}} / {{R|Ω}} = {{C|F}}.

steps.prompt: An integrator with $RC$ = {{RC|s}} starts at $v_o$ = 0. At $t$ = 0 a constant voltage $V$ is applied to its input; the graph shows the output, which saturates at −12 V. Find $V$.
steps.explanation: A constant input gives a ramp with slope $-V/RC$ until the output saturates. The output needs {{tsat|s}} to fall by 12 V, so the slope is 12 V / {{tsat|s}} = {{V/RC}} V/s. Then $V$ = slope × $RC$ = {{V/RC}} V/s × {{RC|s}} = {{V|V}} (positive, since the output goes down).

steps.prompt: A triangle wave (dashed) drives an ideal op-amp **differentiator**. Which graph shows the output (solid)?
steps.explanation: The differentiator gives $v_o = -RC\,dv_{in}/dt$. The triangle has a constant positive slope while it rises and a constant negative slope while it falls, so the output is a square wave: **negative** during the rising parts (because of the minus sign) and positive during the falling parts. An inverted triangle is just an inverting amplifier.

steps.prompt: The triangle wave in the graph is applied to a differentiator with $R$ = {{R|Ω}} and $C$ = {{C|F}}. What is the magnitude of the square-wave output voltage?
steps.explanation: Read the slope of the input: it rises from {{-Vp|V}} to {{Vp|V}} in half a period, {{T/2|s}}, so the slope is {{2*Vp|V}} / {{T/2|s}} = {{4*Vp/T}} V/s. The differentiator gives $|v_o| = RC$ × slope = {{R*C|s}} × {{4*Vp/T}} V/s = {{lev|V}}: negative while the input rises, positive while it falls.
